APart 1 · A · What are we estimating, and why not just pick a model (2011, Sect. 3.1)

What are we estimating? One prediction function

In words: give me a person's baseline information and their activity status, and I predict their 5-year death probability.

  • Data per person: O=(W,A,Y)O=(W,A,Y)O=(W,A,Y). WWW baseline covariates (age, gender, chronic condition), AAA meets the recommended activity level, YYY death within 5 years.
  • P0P_0P0​ is the joint distribution of (W,A,Y)(W,A,Y)(W,A,Y): how WWW is spread, how AAA depends on WWW, how YYY depends on both. We do not know it.
  • The function we want is one feature of P0P_0P0​: the death probability given AAA and WWW.
  • For binary YYY the conditional mean is that probability, so “mean” and “probability” are the same object here.

Line 1: the function. Line 2: the causal risk difference, an average over people of (risk if active) minus (risk if not). Line 3: plug in an estimate and average over the 2066 subjects.

APart 1 · A · What are we estimating, and why not just pick a model (2011, Sect. 3.1)

So which algorithm should I use? We do not know

For any given data set one algorithm is best. Which one depends on the truth, and the truth is what we do not have.

CandidateGood whenLoses when
Logistic regressiontruth is smooth and simpletruth has interactions or curves
Local averagingtruth is roughn is small: too noisy
loess, splinestruth is smooth but not linearwrong span or df
Random forest, boostingtruth is complextruth is simple: extra variance

What counts as an algorithm here

  • Anything that turns a data set into a prediction function: the models above, one method at a fixed tuning value, a screening step plus a predictor. Algorithm and estimator mean the same thing.

The super learner in one sentence

  • Do not pick a winner in advance. Put every reasonable algorithm in a library, let them compete on an objective score, and combine them by performance.

Illustrative weights only. Two things still need defining: the score (Part B) and how the weights are found (Parts C and D).

Sect. 3.1 p. 45 (no a priori best algorithm; definition of algorithm); the same motivation restated in van der Laan and Rose (2018), Targeted Learning in Data Science, Chapter 3, Sect. 3.1 pp. 28–29.5 / 43

BPart 1 · B · What “best” means (2011, Sect. 3.2)

What does “best” mean? First, score one prediction

A loss function says how wrong one prediction is for one person.

A person who actually died (Y = 1)

ModelPredicted P(death)Squared error
Model 10.80(1−0.80)2=0.04(1-0.80)^2=0.04(1−0.80)2=0.04
Model 20.30(1−0.30)2=0.49(1-0.30)^2=0.49(1−0.30)2=0.49
  • Model 1 was closer, so it pays a smaller loss. That is all a loss is: a penalty for one prediction on one person.
  • We choose the loss before seeing the data. It is part of the definition of the problem.
Choosing the loss also chooses what you are estimating (table on the right).

Input: one observation and one candidate function. Output: a number, small is good.

BPart 1 · B · What “best” means (2011, Sect. 3.2)

From one person to the population: risk

Average the loss over everyone who could walk in the door. That average is the score of a candidate function.

  1. Risk = expected loss

    • not a medical risk: the average prediction error under P0P_0P0​

  2. The true function has the smallest risk

    • so the truth can be defined as the risk minimizer

  3. Risk gap = distance to the truth

    • for squared error, exactly the mean squared difference

  4. Best = smaller risk

    • that is the whole definition we needed
The catch: the expectation is under P0P_0P0​, which we do not know.

Line 3 (squared error): the extra risk of a candidate is exactly its squared distance from the truth, averaged over people.

CPart 1 · C · Discrete super learner: a fair contest (2011, Sect. 3.3.1)

The true risk cannot be computed

Section B turned best into smallest risk. But the risk is an average under the true distribution, which we do not have.

Settled so far

  • A loss L(O,ψ)L(O,\psi)L(O,ψ) scores one prediction on one observation; the risk E0L(O,ψ)\E_0 L(O,\psi)E0​L(O,ψ) averages it over the population.
  • Best candidate = smallest risk. The candidate with the smallest risk on the training data is not it: fitting the data you score is cheating.

The open question

How do we estimate each candidate's risk fairly, and then pick one? Section C answers with V-fold cross-validation and the discrete super learner.

On the road map (2011, Fig. 3.5): data → model → target → super learner → TMLE → inference → interpretation. We are inside the super learner box and stay there; TMLE is Chapters 4 and 5.

CPart 1 · C · Discrete super learner: a fair contest (2011, Sect. 3.3.1)

Cross-validation: make every person a stranger to the model

Hide one group, fit on the rest, predict the hidden group, rotate.

  1. Split the 2066 subjects into 10 groups

    • four groups of 206, six of 207

  2. Hide group 1, fit a, b, c on groups 2 to 10

    • predict group 1 with each fit: the values ZZZ

  3. Score group 1

    • loss of each prediction against the real YYY; average within the group

  4. Rotate

    • group 2 hidden, then group 3, … each group is hidden exactly once
Each person is predicted by a model that never saw them. That is the fairness cross-validation buys.
Fig. 3.1 and Sect. 3.3.1 pp. 48–49. Figure redrawn from Fig. 3.1. van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3.9 / 43

DPart 1 · D · Super learner: combine instead of pick (2011, Sect. 3.3.2)

Picking one candidate wastes the others

Section C made the contest fair and picked a winner. The losers still carry information, and the winner is rarely right everywhere.

Settled so far

  • V-fold cross-validation gives every candidate an honest risk: each prediction is scored on people the fit never saw.
  • The discrete super learner keeps the candidate with the smallest cross-validated risk.

The open question

Why throw the others away? Section D learns weights for a combination, by regressing the outcome on the out-of-fold predictions.

On the road map (2011, Fig. 3.5): data → model → target → super learner → TMLE → inference → interpretation. We are inside the super learner box and stay there; TMLE is Chapters 4 and 5.

DPart 1 · D · Super learner: combine instead of pick (2011, Sect. 3.3.2)

A second-layer regression: how much to trust each algorithm

Regress the real outcomes on the three prediction columns. The coefficients are the weights.

  • Predictors are no longer age and gender. They are (Za,Zb,Zc)(Z_a,Z_b,Z_c)(Za​,Zb​,Zc​). Outcome is the real YYY.
  • Result, for example: α=(0.1, 0.7, 0.2)\alpha=(0.1,\,0.7,\,0.2)α=(0.1,0.7,0.2). Numbers are illustrative, not from the book.
  • Weights are nonnegative and sum to one (a convex combination): more stable, and it keeps the blend bounded when each algorithm is bounded.
  • One set of weights for everyone. The piecewise behavior lives inside each algorithm (a random forest already treats young and old differently).
Question for the next slide: the book calls this “minimizing the cross-validated risk”. Where is the cross-validation?

For squared error: make the blended Z columns fit Y as well as possible. For binary Y, Fig. 3.2 writes the family as expit⁡(αaZa+αbZb+αcZc)\expit(\alpha_aZ_a+\alpha_bZ_b+\alpha_cZ_c)expit(αa​Za​+αb​Zb​+αc​Zc​).

αk\alpha_kαk​weight of algorithm kkk; (1,0,0)(1,0,0)(1,0,0) means “use a alone”

DPart 1 · D · Super learner: combine instead of pick (2011, Sect. 3.3.2)

What the theory promises, in plain words

The oracle is the blend a person who knew the truth would choose. Cross-validation gets close to it.

  • Realistic case: no candidate is a correctly specified parametric model. Then the super learner performs asymptotically as well as the best blend in the library, in rate and in the constant.
  • Adding candidates can only help. The guarantee survives even when the library grows polynomially with nnn.
  • Optimistic case: a correct parametric model is in the library. The super learner matches its rate, with a bit more variability.
  • What it does not say: that the super learner beats every base learner in every finite sample. It is an oracle, asymptotic statement.
The super learner is a system for turning many estimators into a better one, and it returns a function you can apply to new patients.

Our choice is at most a little worse than the best candidate, plus a remainder that grows only like log K over n. A big library is cheap.

EPart 1 · E · Does it work (2011, Sect. 3.3.3)

Does it work? Four truths, four different winners

In a simulation we know the truth, so we can measure who gets closest.

  • XXX uniform on [−4,4][-4,4][−4,4], Y=f(X)+UY=f(X)+UY=f(X)+U, UUU standard normal, n=100n=100n=100, repeated 100 times.
  • Steps favor trees. A cubic favors polynomial regression. A sine favors smoothers. The last one is hard for everything.
  • Noise is set so the optimal R2R^2R2 is 0.80 in every panel: same ceiling, fair comparison.
  • Library: 21 algorithms. Same method at different tuning values counts as different candidates: gam at df 2, 3, 4; loess at four spans; nnet at four sizes.
The library was fixed before seeing any of the four truths. Nobody tuned it per panel.

  • Always using bagging wins Sims 1 to 3 and collapses in Sim 4 (0.10).
  • The super learner is never the single best, and never far from it.
  • Sim 4: even the best candidate reaches only 0.54 against a ceiling of 0.80. The library had nothing that fits a fast oscillation.
  • With a richer library the super learner reaches 0.76 (Polley and van der Laan 2010).
The super learner is only as good as its library allows. It finds the best blend of what you gave it; it cannot invent an algorithm you left out.

EPart 1 · E · Does it work (2011, Sect. 3.3.3)

Thirteen real data sets: combining beats choosing

Real data rarely match any single algorithm's form, so the blend should help more than the pick. It does.

Design

  • 13 public data sets, continuous outcomes, nnn from 200 to 654, 3 to 18 covariates (Table 3.3).
  • One fixed library for all: the 21 algorithms plus bayesglm, glmnet, DSA, stepwise, ridge, svm (Table 3.4).
  • Outcomes live on different scales, so compare each algorithm to a linear model on the same data set.

Below 1: better than the linear model. Above 1: worse. Summarized by the geometric mean over the 13 data sets.

Result (Fig. 3.4, 10-fold cross-validated)

  • Super learner beat the discrete super learner; both beat every single algorithm.
  • Best single algorithm was BART, and it still overfit one data set with a relative MSE near 3. The blend had no such blow-up.
  • Plain linear regression ranked only 8th of 20 single algorithms (2018 chapter, p. 29).
  • Learning the weights did not overfit: the honest cross-validated risk of the super learner stayed the lowest.
The benefit showed up with small samples and few covariates. It does not need big data.
Fig. 3.4 and Tables 3.3–3.4 pp. 55–57 (van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3); van der Laan and Rose (2018), Targeted Learning in Data Science, Chapter 3 Sect. 3.1 p. 29.17 / 43

FPart 1 · F · Road maps, and the 2018 chapter's background (2011, Sect. 3.4; 2018, Sect. 3.1)

Two road maps: end point, or first step

Section 3.4 is a “you are here” map. It previews TMLE; it does not teach it.

Prediction question (Fig. 3.6)

  • Data → model → target Q0Q_0Q0​ → bounded loss → super learner → cross-validate the super learner itself.
  • The super learner is the final estimator. Inference by permutation tests is left to the literature.

Effect question (Fig. 3.5)

  • Data → model → target Ψ(P0)\Psi(P_0)Ψ(P0​) → super learner (initial fit of Q0Q_0Q0​) → TMLE → inference → interpretation.
  • The super learner is the middle step. Chapters 4 and 5 do the rest.

What TMLE adds, in one picture

  • An exam has 100 questions, but only question 37 is graded.
  • The super learner studies for the whole exam: Qˉ0(A,W)\bar{Q}_0(A,W)Qˉ​0​(A,W) good everywhere, by prediction loss.
  • TMLE makes a small targeted correction so that question 37, the number Ψ(Q0)\Psi(Q_0)Ψ(Q0​), is answered as well as possible. Still a plug-in, of an updated fit Ψ(Qˉn∗)\Psi(\bar{Q}^*_n)Ψ(Qˉ​n∗​).
An estimator never makes a parameter causal. That reading comes from the model's untestable assumptions.
Sect. 3.4 pp. 59–61 and Figs. 3.5–3.6. The exam analogy is the presenter's. van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3.18 / 43

FPart 1 · F · Road maps, and the 2018 chapter's background (2011, Sect. 3.4; 2018, Sect. 3.1)

The 2018 chapter opens with the same recipe

Same super learner, same guarantee, now aimed at prediction over time.

Notable applications (2018, Sect. 3.1)

SettingWhat the super learner showed
13 public data sets, n = 200 to 654beat every single algorithm; linear regression only 8th of 20 (Polley and van der Laan 2010)
Elderly mortality risk scoresa cohort one-tenth the size of a big health database gave the better function (Rose 2013)
ICU mortality risk scoresAUC 94% where earlier scores validated poorly (Pirracchio et al. 2015)
HIV RNA monitoringflags patients at high risk of virologic failure (Petersen et al. 2015)
Plan payment risk adjustmenta simpler nonparametric formula keeps most of the efficiency (Rose 2016)

What carries over unchanged

  • No algorithm is known in advance to be best, so cross-validate a library and take the optimal weighted average.
  • Section 3.1 restates the finite-sample oracle inequality; Part 2 states it in full and gives the proof idea.
  • New: one regression E(Y∣A,W)\E(Y\mid A,W)E(Y∣A,W) becomes a sequence of regressions run backwards in time, for the target E(Yd∣L0)\E(Y_d\mid L_0)E(Yd​∣L0​).
Prediction and effect estimation stay distinct; LTMLE contains these prediction steps, so the sequential super learner matters for both.

Where Part 1 stopped, and what I will add

Part 1 built one super learner for one problem. Part 2 asks why it works, and how to run it over time.

Part 1 gave us one complete super learner

  • a library of candidates
  • cross-validation to compare them honestly
  • weights from the Z table, refit on all data, combine
  • Key lesson: no single candidate wins everywhere
One example throughout: 5-year death from activity and covariates.

Why a rich library? We do not know the truth

We do not know which world we are in, so we let the candidates compete instead of guessing one.

If the true death risk is …… this candidate tends to win
simple and smoothlogistic regression
smooth but curvedsplines, a GAM
full of interactionsrandom forest, boosting
driven by a few of many covariatesscreening + penalized fit
We do not know which row we are in.
  • No candidate is best for every truth.
  • So aim to be as good as the best in the library.
  • Add every reasonable candidate: several tuning values, several screening rules, experts' own models.
  • The book: do not agonize over which to include. Add them all.
Sect. 3.5, pp. 62–63 (no a priori best estimator for a function-valued parameter; “the free lunch”). van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3.23 / 43
DataTargetLossLibraryCross-validationOutput

Fitting needs one cross-validation, not two

Fitting a super learner needs one cross-validation. The outer loop is only an optional check.

10 folds → Z table → weights 0.1, 0.7, 0.2 → refit on 2066 patients. That is the whole fit.

  • Worried that a big library overfits? Measure it.
  • Hold out an outer fold, run the whole super learner on the rest, score the held-out patients, rotate.
  • The inner weights are thrown away. The final model is trained once, on everyone.
Optional evaluation, not a second model.
Sect. 3.5, p. 63 (“Concerned about overfitting the super learner?”). Sizes in the figure (100 patients, 5 candidates) are illustrative. van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3.24 / 43
DataTargetLossLibraryCross-validationOutput

Choose the loss that matches your question

If you only need pass or fail, you do not need to model the whole score distribution.

Question: this patient's chance of surviving 5 years, Q0(W)=P(T>5∣W)Q_0(W)=P(T>5\mid W)Q0​(W)=P(T>5∣W)

  1. Route A: model the whole survival-time distribution

    • valid, but a much bigger problem than we asked

  2. Route B: define Y∗=I(T>5)Y^*=\mathbb{I}(T>5)Y∗=I(T>5), predict it directly

    • squared error; its minimizer is exactly the 5-year probability

The super learner minimizes the distance its loss defines. Here: the mean squared error of the 5-year probability, nothing else.

Rule: among valid choices, use the simplest loss that directly matches the target you care about.
Sect. 3.5, p. 64 (“Choice of loss function”, survival example); pp. 63–64 for losses with a nuisance parameter (see the cited chapter). van der Laan and Rose (2011), Targeted Learning, Chapter 3.25 / 43

Now the patient is treated twice

One regression is built, defended and proved. From here on the second treatment depends on the first.

Settled so far

The open question

When treatments and conditions alternate over time, what is the target, and why is one regression no longer enough?

On the road map: still the super learner box, now aimed at longitudinal prediction. The targeting step, LTMLE, is the next chapter.

When can we interpret the predictions causally?

The causal interpretation needs three assumptions, in addition to a good prediction model.

01

No unmeasured confounding

At each treatment time, record the common causes of treatment and outcome.

Condition on the history available at that time.

02

Positivity

For histories reached under the rule, its treatment must occur in the data.

03

Consistency

↓

Treatments must be clearly defined.

If a patient follows the rule, their observed outcome equals their outcome under that rule.

HtH_tHt​ denotes the recorded history before treatment AtA_tAt​.

Prediction accuracy alone does not establish these assumptions.

van der Laan and Rose (2018), Targeted Learning in Data Science, Chapter 3, Sect. 3.2 p. 31 (“under a set of strong identifiability assumptions”); the assumptions are set out in the introductory chapters of both books.34 / 43

Averaging over next month's condition, in numbers

At baseline we do not know next month's condition, so we average over it: 0.6 × 0.9 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.74.

This conditional expectation is exactly the averaging in the picture.

  1. After one month: condition known

    • good, not intensified: 0.9; bad, intensified: 0.5

  2. At baseline: not known yet

    • good with 0.6, bad with 0.4; so 0.6 × 0.9 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.74

  3. Population

    • average over the patients

What the chain is for, and what it costs

The cost grows roughly linearly with the number of time points: one full super learner per decision.

Predictionthe chain is the answer

  • Q^1d(L0)\hat Q^d_{1}(L_0)Q^​1d​(L0​): the doctor's number, per patient, per rule. Its average estimates E(Yd)\E(Y_d)E(Yd​).

Effectthe chain is the initial fit

  • LTMLE (Chapter 4) starts from these regressions and adds a targeting step at each time point.

Computation (Sect. 3.4)

3 candidates, 5 folds: 18 fits per decision, 36 for two, 90 for five. Candidates fit independently: parallelize.

van der Laan and Rose (2018), Targeted Learning in Data Science, Chapter 3, Sect. 3.4 (p. 34) and Sect. 3.5 (p. 34); chapter introduction p. 28 on the stand-alone role and LTMLE; road map after 2011 Fig. 3.5.42 / 43

Main points

Why the super learner is allowed to be greedy

  1. Cross-validation picks nearly as well as an oracle that knows the true risk, and a bigger library costs only log K.

  2. If the validation risk is close to the true risk for every candidate, the validation winner is close to the true winner. That is the whole proof.

How the same machine runs backward in time

  1. Every step backward replaces the future by its conditional mean: the previous predicted probability becomes the new outcome.

  2. L1L_1L1​ is averaged out, not ignored: it lives inside the outcome column, not among the inputs.

The Super Learner itself only needs one cross-validation, which learns the weights. But if we want an honest estimate of how the whole procedure does on new data, we can add an outer loop.

Let's say we have one hundred patients. We hold out ten of them, and on the other ninety, we fit a complete Super Learner, with its own inner loop. Then we predict the ten held-out patients and record their losses, and we repeat this until everyone has been held out once. The average of those losses tells us how well the whole procedure predicts for new patients.

The fits inside the outer loop are only for evaluation. At the end, we train once more on all one hundred patients, and that's the model we actually use.

Okay, so we can have a large library. But why should cross-validation make a good choice from it? That's what the oracle guarantee is about.

Imagine someone who knows the true distribution. For every fitted candidate, they can compute its true risk, and they just pick the lowest one. We call that the oracle choice, and it's the best we can do inside this library.

Cross-validation has the same goal, but it only has the held-out data, so it picks what looks best there. The two choices can be different, and the question is how much we lose.

Here ddd means excess risk, which is a candidate's risk minus the risk of the truth, Q0Q_0Q0​.

The formal result below has two parts. There's a factor close to one in front of the oracle risk, and there's an extra term of order log⁡K/(np)\log K / (np)logK/(np). Here KKK is the number of candidates, and npnpnp is the size of the validation sample.

So this term grows slowly when we add candidates, and it gets smaller when the sample grows. So the price we pay for choosing is small.

The proof has three steps, and we'll start with one candidate.

So step one is about one candidate and one split. We fit the candidate on the training data, and then we hold that fitted function fixed. So the validation patients are new data for this function.

For each validation patient, we take the candidate's loss minus the loss at the truth, and we call it XXX. The average of XXX is d^(k)\hat d(k)d^(k), and its population mean is d(k)d(k)d(k), the true excess risk.

But the validation set is only a sample, so d^(k)\hat d(k)d^(k) can be a little above or a little below d(k)d(k)d(k).

Bernstein's inequality gives us a bound on the probability of a large gap. As you can see in the curve, with more validation data, a large gap becomes less likely.

We need two conditions here. The loss differences are bounded, and their variance is controlled by the excess risk itself. In other words, when a candidate is close to the truth, its loss difference also varies less, and that's what gives us the fast rate.

Now we apply it at the bottom. We allow a gap of δ d(k)+ε\delta\, d(k) + \varepsilonδd(k)+ε, so there's a relative part and an absolute part. And the chance of a bigger gap drops very fast as np εnp\,\varepsilonnpε grows.

So for one candidate, the validation risk is close to the true risk, with high probability.

Now step two. So far, we fixed one candidate in advance. But Super Learner looks at all of them and then chooses. A candidate can look good just by chance, and that may be the one we pick. So we need the bound to hold for every candidate at the same time.

Each candidate has a small chance of missing its bound. The chance that at least one of them misses is at most the sum. So with KKK candidates, we get KKK times the single bound. This is the union bound.

Then on the right, we ask that the total failure probability stays below a small number, η\etaη, and we solve for ε\varepsilonε. Taking the log turns KKK into log⁡K\log KlogK, and dividing by the validation size gives us log⁡K/(np)\log K / (np)logK/(np).

So this penalty shows up because we're choosing among many candidates. And since log⁡K\log KlogK grows very slowly, a much larger library costs only a little more.

Before we go to the numbers, I should mention that if we want to read the result causally, as what would happen if patients followed the rule, we need three assumptions.

The first is no unmeasured confounding. At each treatment time, we have recorded the common causes of treatment and outcome.

The second is positivity. For the histories we reach under the rule, some patients in the data actually got the treatment the rule assigns. Otherwise, there's nothing to learn from.

The third is consistency. The treatments are clearly defined, and if a patient follows the rule, their observed outcome is their outcome under the rule.

Super Learner helps us estimate the regressions well, but it can't give us these assumptions.

If there are more treatment times, we don't need anything new. We fit a Super Learner, apply the rule, and save the predictions. Then we move one treatment time earlier and repeat.

The inputs get shorter as we move toward baseline, because less history is available.

So what do we use this for? The first use is prediction. For a patient's baseline, the final fit gives the chance of success under a rule, and we can do this for several rules and compare them.

The second use is as a starting point. Longitudinal TMLE begins with these regressions and adds a targeting step, which is the next chapter.

So let me sum up. The first point is that cross-validation picks almost as well as an oracle, and a bigger library only costs log⁡K\log KlogK.

The second point is the proof. If the validation risk is close to the true risk for every candidate, then the validation winner is close to the true winner.

The third point is about time. We go backward, and at each step, the last prediction becomes the new outcome.

And the last point is that L1L_1L1​ is averaged out, not ignored, because it's already in the outcome column.

So if we put the two parts together, Part 1 showed how one Super Learner works, and Part 2 showed why it works, and how we can run it over time.

I think the main thing to remember is that we don't have to pick one model in advance. We can put many candidates in the library and let cross-validation decide, and the same idea still works when treatment happens more than once.
